The proposal study is a factorial comparison, with the score estimator held
fixed while proposal quality is measured. Its proposal families are bootstrap,
locally adapted, KDM, LEDH/GenUT, twisted PF, iAPF, SGQF-guided, and defensive
mixtures. Crossed factors are lookahead (none, fixed one-step, iterated $\psi$),
covariance ($P^Q$, UKF, KDM, LEDH, SGQF, and calibrated hybrid), particle count,
horizon, and observation regime. Model-corrected normalizer MSE is the primary
criterion for a normalizer-accuracy claim. A better-score claim requires lower
oracle score MSE at the declared particle or compute budget, after the proposal
identity and target-preservation tests pass. Coefficient of variation of
$\widehat z_t$, effective sample size, and weight tails explain the result;
they do not replace score error as the criterion.
The linear-Gaussian/Kalman model is the first oracle-bearing check; nonlinear
regular-transition models and high-dimensional SGQF cases follow.

Hard vetoes are a missing or non-integrable proposal density, support failure,
non-finite or incorrectly corrected weights, use of an approximate SGQF or
twisted likelihood as the target, and a claim route that cannot be traced to the
declared proposal. A paired uncertainty analysis is required before calling a
candidate better. A passing proposal test establishes a viable proposal arm;
it does not establish an unbiased score.

\begin{proposition}[Symmetric cubic derivative weights]
\label{prop:fd-cubic-weights}
For the eleven equally spaced nodes in \eqref{eq:fd-cubic-fit}, define
$S_r=\sum_{j=-5}^{5}j^r$. The fitted derivative is
\begin{equation}
 D_3(h;v)=\frac1h\sum_{j=-5}^{5}c_j\widehat\ell(\theta+jhv),\qquad
 c_j=\frac{S_6j-S_4j^3}{S_2S_6-S_4^2},\qquad
 (S_2,S_4,S_6)=(110,1958,41030).          \label{eq:fd-cubic-weights}
\end{equation}
For a deterministic $f\in C^5$, the leading errors are
$D_4-f'(0)=-f^{(5)}(0)h^4/30+o(h^4)$ and
$D_3-f'(0)=-143f^{(5)}(0)h^4/90+o(h^4)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Symmetry separates the odd and even columns of the least-squares design.
Fitting against the dimensionless columns $j$ and $j^3$ gives the odd normal
matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}S_2&S_4\\S_4&S_6\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Its first inverse row gives $c_j$; division by $h$ converts the fitted
coefficient to a derivative. Hence $\sum c_j=0$, $\sum jc_j=1$,
$\sum j^2c_j=\sum j^3c_j=\sum j^4c_j=0$.
Taylor expansion leaves $h^4 f^{(5)}(0)\sum j^5c_j/5!$.
The last sum divided by $5!$ is $-143/90$. Applying the same calculation to
the coefficients $(1,-8,0,8,-1)/12$ at $j=(-2,-1,0,1,2)$ gives $-1/30$.
\end{proof}
Thus more points do not give a higher formal order. The eleven-point cubic fit
has a different truncation constant and a different response to correlated
likelihood noise; a symmetric linear or quadratic fit generally retains an
$O(h^2)$ term.

\begin{proposition}[Symmetric cubic derivative weights]
\label{prop:fd-cubic-weights}
For the eleven equally spaced nodes in \eqref{eq:fd-cubic-fit}, define
$S_r=\sum_{j=-5}^{5}j^r$. The fitted derivative is
\begin{equation}
 D_3(h;v)=\frac1h\sum_{j=-5}^{5}c_j\widehat\ell(\theta+jhv),\qquad
 c_j=\frac{S_6j-S_4j^3}{S_2S_6-S_4^2},\qquad
 (S_2,S_4,S_6)=(110,1958,41030).          \label{eq:fd-cubic-weights}
\end{equation}
For a deterministic $f\in C^5$, the leading errors are
$D_4-f'(0)=-f^{(5)}(0)h^4/30+o(h^4)$ and
$D_3-f'(0)=-143f^{(5)}(0)h^4/90+o(h^4)$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Symmetry separates the odd and even columns of the least-squares design.
Fitting against the dimensionless columns $j$ and $j^3$ gives the odd normal
matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}S_2&S_4\\S_4&S_6\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Its first inverse row gives $c_j$; division by $h$ converts the fitted
coefficient to a derivative. Hence $\sum c_j=0$, $\sum jc_j=1$,
$\sum j^2c_j=\sum j^3c_j=\sum j^4c_j=0$.
Taylor expansion leaves $h^4 f^{(5)}(0)\sum j^5c_j/5!$.
The last sum divided by $5!$ is $-143/90$. Applying the same calculation to
the coefficients $(1,-8,0,8,-1)/12$ at $j=(-2,-1,0,1,2)$ gives $-1/30$.
\end{proof}
Thus more points do not give a higher formal order. The eleven-point cubic fit
has a different truncation constant and a different response to correlated
likelihood noise; a symmetric linear or quadratic fit generally retains an
$O(h^2)$ term.

candidate better. A passing proposal test establishes a viable proposal arm;
it does not establish an unbiased score.
